t: Check If String Is a Prefix of Array — Concatenate Until You Match or Overshoot
o: We must decide whether s can be formed by gluing together the first k strings of words for some positive k: only a prefix of the array may be used, and every word used must be used whole. In Example 1, concatenating "i", "love", and "leetcode" produces exactly "iloveleetcode", so the answer is true — we stop there even though a fourth word remains unused. In Example 2 the array starts with "apples", so every possible concatenation begins with a, p, ... which can never match "iloveleetcode"; the answer is false. The constraints are tiny (at most 100 words of length up to 20, |s| up to 1000), so any linear scan over the involved characters is fast enough; the only real trap is that s must end exactly at a word boundary, never in the middle of a word.
k: A valid match ends exactly on a word boundary — s being a prefix of the full concatenation is necessary but not sufficient.
Once the running concatenation becomes longer than s, failure is certain because words are appended whole, never truncated.
Early exit keeps the scan cheap: compare when lengths coincide, bail when they overshoot.

a.n: Approach 1: Accumulate Words and Compare at Boundaries
a.i: Keep appending words to a growing buffer. The moment its length equals len(s), the candidate prefix concatenation is complete, so the answer is whether it equals s. If it overshoots len(s), fail immediately — later appends only make it longer. If the words run out first, s is longer than any prefix concatenation could ever be.
s: Append the next word to the buffer.
If the buffer length equals len(s), return whether buffer == s.
If the buffer length exceeds len(s), return false.
If all words are consumed without either condition firing, return false.
a.t: O(|s| + L) — every character of s and of the consumed words is touched once, where L is the total length of words used before terminating
a.sp: O(L) — the accumulated copy of the matched words

a.n: Approach 2: Character Walk Without Building Strings
a.i: Walk s with an index while sweeping through the words one at a time. Every character of the current word must equal the corresponding character of s, and finishing a word exactly when the index reaches the end of s means success. This variant needs no concatenated copy at all.
s: Keep index i into s, starting at 0.
For each word, advance through its characters, failing if i leaves s or any character mismatches.
After finishing a word, return true immediately if i == len(s).
Return false once all words are exhausted.
a.t: O(|s| + L) — same linear scan as Approach 1 minus the string-building cost

w: Either approach is a solid interview answer; state the boundary rule up front since it is the only subtle part. Pitfalls: declaring victory when s matches only part of the full concatenation (words = ["ab"], s = "a"), forgetting that k must be positive (s can never equal the empty concatenation), and off-by-one errors when s ends mid-word. Follow-ups: allow skipping or reusing words (becomes a matching problem), or require s to equal the concatenation of the entire array (then a plain equality check suffices).
